svg.text: Where each tire runs out, drawn on the road it happens on

The same corner driven twice, identical in every respect except which axle is driven. The car is drawn at five points along its own solved line; each contact patch is coloured by how much of that tire is left.
Arrow length is how much of the tire is spent; arrow direction is what it was spent on. Long and diagonal is the expensive one.
fraction of the tire being used:
nothing left to steer or brake with at 100%
Follow the front wheels along each line. Through the corner both cars are the same: all four patches near the top of the scale, because both
are cornering as hard as the tires allow and the lines are nearly identical.
Past the corner exit they part company. The rear-drive car's front patches cool off — the corner is over, they are only steering. The
front-drive car's stay hot, and its arrows stay long and diagonal, because the same two tires that are finishing the corner are also the
ones putting the power down. Over this corner and the straight after it that costs -0.03 s.
Cropped to 40–191 m along the track; scale 58 px per 10 m. The car is drawn about 1.8× its true size so the wheels are legible — positions, headings and steer angles are to scale.

[MEASURED] double-track model + optimal control + Sedan_Pac02Tire.tir - offsets removed - m 1360 kg - 54% front - 100 nodes - [SOURCED] RV-1 params §1 - IDEAL differential [ASSUMED]: torque split floats freely, the best an LSD could manage. See figure 03 for the open-diff case
Contact-patch size is vertical load, normalised per instant; patch colour and arrow length are friction-circle usage. Slip angle is constrained to ±12° and envelope occupancy is zero in both solves.
